newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil gov't calm over current account gap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil gov't calm over current account gap.

text.p: Brazil's Central Bank Monday struck a relaxed pose over the country's widening current account gap, saying the expansion in the deficit was not "explosive" and easily financed by foreign investment.

Altamir Lopes, head of the bank's economics department, also added his voice to the rest of the Brazilian government's economics team, insisting the recent currency woes of some Asian nations might actually benefit Brazil.
One of the things Brazil shares with those countries is a widening current account gap, which reached 4.2 percent of gross domestic product in the 12 months to end-June.
"I don't know exactly where it's going to go, but the trend is for it to expand further," Lopes said.

"Everything depends on how you finance the gap. It also depends on the manner in which the gap grows," he added. "There's nothing explosive about this growth. Secondly, we're basically financing it with direct investment."
Foreign direct investment of $7.4 billion in the first half of 1997 covered about 47 percent of the balance of payments current account deficit in that period, the bank said.

Lopes reiterated predictions of some $15 billion in foreign direct investment for this year, which he said would cover at least 40 percent of the current account shortfall, generally seen widening to some 4.5 percent of GDP by December.

Over the past two weeks, Thailand and the Philippines have been forced into de facto devaluations by speculative attacks on their currencies. Nerves in emerging countries markets were rattled and the Malaysian and Indonesian currencies have also come under pressure.
Besides its bloated current account gap, analysts say Brazil suffers another of the elements that made the Asian countries vulnerable -- a currency generally regarded as overvalued.
But Brazilian officials have rejected the possibility of any spillover akin to the "Tequila effect" of Mexico's disastrous peso devaluation in 1994.
Finance Minister Pedro Malan said over the weekend the forex woes in Asia might undermine confidence in emerging markets.

But he said, according to the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper, that they could also boost Brazil because its current account deficit was much lower and its privatization program was in full swing, assuring plenty of foreign direct investment.
The Central Bank's Director of International Affairs, Gustavo Franco, said last week anything bad for Brazil's competitors could be good for Brazil.
"Foreign capital may decide to come here instead," Franco said through a spokeswoman.
On Monday, Lopes joined the fray.
"If capital pulls out of those markets, it will find somewhere else to go to," he said.

Lopes also pointed out that the Central Bank believes its foreign exchange rate system, based on two currency bands supported by Central Bank simultaneous buy-sell operations, was "flexible" enough to withstand any speculative attacks.
Brazil also has $57 billion in reserves to draw on if it needs to defend the real currency.
